newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe rate cut seen boosting business.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe rate cut seen boosting business.

text.p: The cut of 3.5 percentage points in the Zimbabwe Reserve Bank's rediscount rate, effective last Friday, could see commercial banks lower lending rates this week and stimulate business activity, economists and dealers said on Monday.
They said that the sizeable rate cut to 23.5 percent from 27 percent had been widely expected and sent an obvious message to Zimbabwe's commercial banks that lending rates were too high.
"It's a very deep cut but it gives a clear message to commercial banks that they can now reduce lending rates," private economic consultant John Robertson told Reuters.
"I would say we are likely to see that during the course of this week," he added.
Last October commercial banks' lending rates fell below 30 percent for the first time in five years -- with the country's biggest bank Standard Chartered Zimbabwe offering 28.5 percent.

Robertson said lower rates would bring a change in the whole nature of business decisions. "High rates mean that people don't take risks. Now that the interest rates are down, people who would usually put their money into banks will now spend it," he said.

Recent lower inflation rates in Zimbabwe had made it just a matter of time before the rediscount rate -- the rate at which commercial banks borrow money from the central bank -- was reduced, money market dealers said.
Annual inflation dropped to a seven-year low last November of 13.9 percent before rising to 16.4 percent in December.
Robertson forecasts January's figure to be 15.8 percent.

"It (the rate cut) is an indication of the Reserve Bank's medium- and long-term view on inflation. The rediscount rate was too high in light of inflation and the money market rates," said a money market dealer who asked not to be identified.
He added that the rate cut would have no immediate effect on the money market, but those rates would drop soon.
Robertson said that the drop in the rediscount rate would further reduce inflation.

"In the initial stages, lower rates mean reduced rates for many businesses and they won't feel such a need to put prices up. It will mean cost reduction and therefore will hold the rate of increase in inflation down," he said.
"But whether it's 23 percent or 16 percent, we still have a high rate of inflation," he added.
